sources.news_title: US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
sources.text:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
The Department of Justice has faced criticism that its lawsuit is aimed at blocking a Democratic victory in a key race.
United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the Department of Justice’s decision to sue to prevent the certification of a Republican loss in Alaska’s tight Senate race.
On Sunday, Blanche did a tour of the morning political shows in the US, making stops at CNN’s State of the Union TV programme and CBS’s Face the Nation.
In each appearance, he faced pointed questions about the legality of the Justice Department’s efforts, responding, in some cases, with open frustration.
“ Why is this controversial?” Blanche asked CNN host Dana Bash at one point. He proceeded to accuse one of the candidates in the Senate race of intentionally trying to confuse voters.
“We’re going to try to create a situation where that can be remedied,” he said. “That shouldn’t be something that is causing this shock and horror.”
But the Justice Department’s lawsuit, filed on October 22, has been the subject of bipartisan criticism.
Many have accused President Donald Trump’s administration of laying the groundwork to block a Democratic win in the race. Trump himself claimed to have authorised the lawsuit.
“I’m the one who said do it,” he told reporters on Friday.
Inside the Alaska Senate race
During the November 3 midterm elections, citizens in Alaska will vote in one of the country’s closest Senate races, which will help decide whether Republicans maintain their majority in the chamber.
Senator Dan S Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is seeking to defend his seat in the US Senate. But he faces fierce competition from former US Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
Also in the running is Dan J Sullivan, a former Forest Service employee.
The second Sullivan’s decision to run has raised concerns that he is a spoiler candidate, whose presence on the ballot is designed to draw votes away from the incumbent.
But the Forest Service worker has denied any such intent. Such allegations, he said, are “entirely false”.
“I am not a registered Democrat, and I have had no conversations whatsoever with the Peltola campaign about my candidacy,” the second Sullivan wrote in a letter to Alaska’s lieutenant governor before the state’s primaries.
“I have considered running for political office for over a decade. I made the decision to formally run for the United States Senate in the upcoming primary election because Senator Sullivan has routinely failed the people of Alaska, and they deserve a better representative. It is my right to do so.”
Four candidates advanced to the final round of voting after Alaska’s August primaries. They included Peltola and both Sullivans. The two men are running as Republicans.
A controversial lawsuit
The Justice Department has argued that its lawsuit – filed less than two weeks before the midterm elections – is necessary “to protect the integrity” of the election.
Any result in the Senate race, it argues, would be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan”.
The department has therefore called on the US District Court in Alaska to issue an order declaring the race’s certification “unlawful” and barring the state from “allowing such a certification to occur”.
Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections, though Congress has the right to pass regulations concerning federal votes.
It is highly unusual for a presidential administration to inject itself into issues of state election certification, and experts say such a move is likely to be deemed illegal.
Already in June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that both Sullivans could compete in the Senate race. The state’s Division of Elections has also taken steps to reduce voter confusion.
The November 3 ballot, for instance, will list Dan S Sullivan as the incumbent and as a “registered Republican”.
Dan J Sullivan, meanwhile, will have the suffix “Jr” added to his name, and his party affiliation will be left blank, despite the candidate identifying as Republican.
But in Sunday’s television appearances, Blanche, who leads the Department of Justice and formerly served as Trump’s personal lawyer, argued that merely having two Sullivans on the ballot is a recipe for confusion.
“It is wrong,” Blanche told CNN. “Putting aside whether we’re going to win or lose in the courts, putting aside what the Alaskan Supreme Court has done, in our system, we should not have a candidate who has to worry about another candidate being on the ballot for no other reason than to confuse voters.”
Blanche also denied any impropriety in Trump saying he ordered the lawsuit.
“He’s supposed to make sure that everything in this country is running right, including elections,” Blanche said.
The race for the Senate
Historically, the Justice Department has embraced a norm of judicial independence, though critics have accused the Trump administration of wielding its prosecutorial powers for political gain.
Bash, the CNN host, raised some of those concerns, pointing to Trump’s comments accusing Democrats of cheating, as well as his history of election denialism.
The president has long denied his loss in the 2020 presidential race, and his supporters sought to block the certification of the election, notably by storming the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.
When Bash pointed to that incident, Blanche chided her: “Oh, you’ve got to stop it with that.”
“Why are you yelling at me?” Bash responded as the two talked over each other.
“You are not being a real person. Come on, man,” Blanche continued. “That is crazy.”
He also denied that Trump was setting the stage for a contested election if the Democrat, Peltola, were to win. Instead, he framed the lawsuit as setting the stage for further investigations into any eventual results.
“The relief that we’re seeking – which, again, isn’t to determine who the senator is, it’s not to try to overturn something the state is going to do – it’s just to make sure that the ballots that come in are kept in a way that may allow a court to investigate further,” Blanche said.
Speaking to CBS, Blanche also dodged a question about whether Trump personally asked him to file the lawsuit.
“I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States. I never have, and I never will,” Blanche said.
The race to control the US Senate is expected to be a nail-biter, with Republicans holding a slim majority at present: They have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.
Only a third of the Senate’s seats – 35 in total – will be up for grabs in the midterm races, though, as terms in the chamber last six years and are staggered across different election years.
Trump’s Republican Party is projected to face an uphill battle to protect its congressional majorities amid backlash against the rising cost of living and Trump’s withering poll numbers.
Roughly seven Senate elections are considered toss-ups, including the Alaska race.
In early October, The New York Times and Siena College released a poll suggesting Peltola is leading incumbent Sullivan by nearly 7 percentage points, one of the widest margins of any of the toss-up states.

sources.news_title: Blanche defends Trump-ordered lawsuit over Alaska Senate election certification
sources.text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department's lawsuit on Sunday seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
The lawsuit, filed last week, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion over the name Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher also on the ballot. The DOJ said confusion over the two Sullivans could help former Alaska Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who is narrowly ahead in polls just over a week from Election Day, win the election.
"What we're asking the court to do is make sure that after the election, if it's clear that there was confusion, if it's clear, and that's for a court to decide at a later date if there's litigation ... and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voter, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing," Blanche said on CNN's "State of the Union."
"Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try and thwart and cheat in an election as they're doing in this case," he said.
The DOJ's lawsuit says that the potential for voter confusion exists and Alaska should not certify the election if "(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election."
Alaska applies a top-four primary system to select candidates for the general election. The November general election uses ranked-choice voting.
Ranked-choice voting lets voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of votes in the first round of counting, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Voters who ranked the eliminated candidate first then have their second choice counted and added to that candidate's total. This continues until a majority winner — or the candidate with more than half of the vote — wins.
Republicans have argued for months that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to confuse voters and have sought to remove him from the ballot. Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the candidate, and Sullivan himself has denied running to confuse voters.
The Alaska Division of Elections briefly removed Daniel J. Sullivan in June, before a state court ordered his name returned to the ballot. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision.
President Donald Trump, who has long made claims of voter fraud without evidence, said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit himself.
Democratic groups and voting rights advocates, including Peltola's campaign, are seeking to join the lawsuit to stop the DOJ's effort to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan loses. The groups argue the executive branch lacks the legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration, with early voting already underway.
"In an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections, the Department of Justice—acting on the President's personal orders—demands that this Court enjoin the certification of the ongoing U.S. Senate election, but only if the President's preferred candidate loses," the motion to intervene reads. "But the federal government has no power to impose that Hobson's choice on the people of this State."
Alaska is seen as one of the best chances for a Democratic flip in the Nov. 3 elections, which will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's term. Trump has been barnstorming competitive states in recent weeks as the polls favor Democrats to win control of the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate.
Democrats and voting rights advocates have long feared that Trump — who denied his election loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020, leading to a violent riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — would attempt to meddle in the midterm contest to save narrow Republican majorities in Congress.
Blanche bristled on Sunday when asked whether the lawsuit aimed to sway the election in Alaska toward Republicans.
"That is crazy," Blanche said, pressed on CNN about whether the president is laying the groundwork for a "doomsday" scenario in which he tries to overturn election results.
"We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that ... the groundwork that we are laying is for the state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be."

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Trump administration’s lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race and argued that the legal challenge was a necessary step to avoid confusing voters in the closely watched midterm race.

“At least let him use the name Sen. Dan Sullivan as opposed to incumbent, because a lot of people don’t know what incumbent means,” Trump said.
Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
Blanche represented Trump as a personal attorney before the Republican president appointed him to lead the Department of Justice, which filed the lawsuit in Alaska. Blanche defended Trump in his election inference case before voters elected Trump to a second White House term, effectively ending the criminal prosecution.
Blanche told CNN host Dana Bash that it was “crazy” for her to ask him if Trump was trying to lay the groundwork for the same sort of election challenges that occurred before a mob of his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
“We are not doing anything improper. We’re not doing anything we’re not allowed to do. And we have to let the process play out,” Blanche said. “But I do think it’s important for the American people to understand that we are not — (and) President Trump is not — trying to take over a state election in any way shape or form.”
The lawsuit, he told CBS’ “Face the Nation,” is meant to “put guardrails in place” to preserve possible evidence of voter confusion at the polls.
“It’s not saying, ‘Don’t certify.’ It’s saying, ‘If a court ultimately determines that it was decided because of confusion and not the will of the voters, then we do not think the states should certify.’ And that’s consistent with federal law and consistent with even Alaskan law, if that happens,” he said.

Todd Blanche Tells CNN Host 'That Is Not a Real Question' Amid Row Over Trump's Alaska Senate Election Lawsuit
The US attorney general says the Justice Department case aims to preserve ballots and allow courts to examine possible voter confusion, not overturn the result
US Attorney General Todd Blanche rejected uggestions on Sunday, 25 October, that President Donald Trump was laying the groundwork to overturn election results through an Alaska Senate election lawsuit.
Speaking on CNN's State of the Union, Blanche challenged host Dana Bash's questioning, declaring, 'That is not, that is not a real question.'
The confrontation followed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska's Senate election under certain circumstances if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses.
The controversy centres on another candidate also named Dan Sullivan, whose middle initial differs from the incumbent's.
Blanche insisted the lawsuit was intended to preserve ballots and allow courts to investigate potential voter confusion, rather than interfere with election results.
Todd Blanche Rejects Questions Over Alaska Senate Election Lawsuit
During Sunday's interview, Bash questioned whether the legal challenge could lead to a confrontation resembling the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election.
Her question referenced the events of 6 January 2021, when Trump supporters attacked the US Capitol following his election defeat.
Blanche rejected the comparison, accusing Bash of misrepresenting the Justice Department's intentions.
'You set me up with the following question: Because the Department of Justice is concerned that there's an absolute fraud happening in Alaska, and he wants to do something about it, you're saying, 'Mr. Attorney General, because the president of the United States wants to stop a fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he gonna do something crazy?' That is not, that is not a real question,' Blanche said.
The attorney general maintained that any decision concerning election irregularities would rest with the courts rather than Trump.
'What I said is the groundwork that we are laying is for Alaska, for the state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be. That is not Donald J. Trump. That is not our president,' he added.
The supplied account provides no independent evidence establishing fraud or confirming that voters have been deliberately misled.
Trump's Admission Raises Questions About Todd Blanche's Defence
The controversy intensified after Trump publicly acknowledged encouraging the Justice Department's legal challenge.
'Well, I'm the one that said 'do it,'' Trump told reporters in Florida on Friday when questioned about the lawsuit.
Despite the president's admission, Blanche declined to confirm whether Trump directly ordered him to file the case. He maintained that his private communications with the president were not matters for public discussion.
Blanche also defended Trump's allegations that Democrats were 'cheating' through the Alaska ballot arrangements. Those allegations remain unsubstantiated in the supplied account.
'He's not admitting it's political,' Blanche said. 'He's the executive. He's supposed to make sure that there's, everything in this country is running right, including elections.'
The attorney general previously maintained that he did not intend to intervene in the midterm election certification process. However, he acknowledged the possibility of a 'doomsday scenario' requiring Justice Department action.
For now, the lawsuit concerns a potential certification dispute rather than an established election irregularity. Whether the courts will need to examine the disputed ballot arrangements depends on what happens when Alaska voters cast their ballots.

sources.news_title: 'Total gobbledygook': Trump DOJ roasted for nonsense election meddling
sources.text:
President Donald Trump's Attorney General attempted to defend the administration's latest bombshell election lawsuit, prompting a thorough roasting from observers across social media, with one prominent New York Times columnist calling his argument "total gobbledygook."
The Justice Department this week filed a lawsuit asking a federal court to block the certification of Alaska's Senate race if incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan loses by a small enough margin. The agency alleged that too much confusion was being created by the presence of another third-party candidate also named Dan Sullivan on the ballot, despite the fact that the state's Supreme Court allowed the situation to play out months ago.
Critics warned that this was an effort to meddle with the lawful results of the race, where polls show Democratic nominee Mary Peltola poised to flip that seat, despite Alaska's red state reputation.
Attorney General Todd Blanche appeared on CBS News Sunday, where he was pressed to defend the DOJ's Alaska suit. He argued that the agency is "asking the court to step in where the Alaska Supreme Court didn't, which is to look at federal law and, if necessary, to allow a process for Alaska to decide who should be certified as the winner," despite the fact that elections themselves are what decided who gets certified.
Blanche's excuse was met with more scrutiny from critics, with liberal NYT columnist Jamelle Bouie arguing on BlueSky that his explanation was complete nonsense and further exposed the Trump administration's midterm desperation.
"This is total gobbledygook? The process to decide who should be certified as the winner is the election, and there is no federal law that says the courts get to decide who that is," Bouie posted. "This interview is a real sign that they are just throwing s—— and desperately hoping that it sticks."
Bouie also later responded to a clip from Blanche's Sunday appearance on CNN, where host Dana Bash asked what the crime is that they are targeting in Alaska. Blanche argued only that there could potentially be a crime, and that Alaskans being confused was the main issue, to which Bash stressed that the state Supreme Court had already litigated the issue.
"You know, I think this guy might be bad at the law," Bouie added.
Former Republican media consultant Matthew Scheffield responded to Bouie's thread, adding: "It's even dumber since ranked choice voting, which Trump says is a scam even though it led to him winning in Alaska 3 times, eliminates any confusion over Dan Sullivans since you can just rank the other one second. This rhetoric is not supposed to make sense. It's supposed to create confusion."
Bradley P. Moss, a lawyer based in Washington, D.C., also responded to a clip of Blanche's argument on CNN, saying that it reveals how much "They have nothing" to work with when it comes to meddling with the midterms.

AG Todd Blanche says DOJ is "doing our own research under the law" with Alaska Senate challenge
sources.text:
AG Todd Blanche says DOJ is "doing our own research under the law" with Alaska Senate challenge
Washington — Attorney General Todd Blanche said Sunday that the Justice Department was looking to "put guardrails in place" with its move to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if there is evidence that voters were confused by a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
"This is the Department of Justice doing our own research under the law," Blanche said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
The Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week to preemptively challenge the certification of Alaska's Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, loses. Sullivan is facing off against Democratic candidate Mary Peltola in next week's election, in a race that has appeared closer than initially expected in a state that President Trump won in 2024 by double digits. But the state has a top-four primary and ranked-choice voting election system, with another candidate adding a wrinkle to the race.
Daniel J. Sullivan, a former teacher who shares the same first and last name with the sitting senator, announced in June that he was entering the race, prompting a push by the incumbent senator to remove him from the ballot. That month, an Alaska election official determined he was not eligible to appear on the ballot, citing a "determined effort and a deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. But the challenger appealed the decision, and the state Supreme Court later affirmed that he could appear on the ballot, paving the way for both Sullivans' names to appear.
Blanche emphasized Sunday that the DOJ's lawsuit is "not saying, 'don't certify.'" But if a court determined that the race was decided "because of confusion, and not the will of the voters," then the Justice Department does not think the state should certify the election.
The attorney general argued that it may "be obvious from the results and from the ballots that voters were confused," though he acknowledged that "we don't know what's going to happen yet."
"That could be obvious from the way that they rank the Dan Sullivans, or not including a Dan Sullivan on the ballot, I don't know yet because there hasn't been an election," Blanche said. "But all we are doing is trying to put guardrails in place so that if that happens, there's a system allowed where the ballots are kept in a way so that we can determine whether there was confusion."
Pressed on why the challenge was filed 11 days before Election Day, Blanche said the administration had hoped that the state Supreme Court "would actually issue an opinion and explain their reasoning." He said that it's an issue the president has been talking about for months, saying, "This isn't something new that just came up last week."
Asked Friday about the Justice Department's lawsuit, Mr. Trump told reporters, "Well, I'm the one that said, 'do it.'" Blanche said he had "no idea" to whom the president was referring, and would not discuss his own personal communications with the president.
Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican who also appeared on "Face the Nation" on Sunday, said he thinks it's appropriate "to take a look at" the situation in Alaska.
"I'm not sure why they thought they had to file a lawsuit, other than as Todd said earlier, make sure that you have the ballots right so we can be certain that the Democrats were not successful in confusing candidates to vote for someone else to better position Peltola for being the winner," Tillis said.
The comments came after GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski, Alaska's other senator, on Friday said she was opposed to the Justice Department's move.
"Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot," Murkowski wrote in a post on X. "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."
The sitting senator's name will be noted as "(Registered Republican) Incumbent" on the ballot.
Asked about Murkowski's comments, Tillis said, "there are very few people that know Alaska better than Lisa."
Tillis said he doesn't mind "looking at it," but "I do mind the appearance of filing a lawsuit before we even know if the facts that would substantiate a lawsuit actually occur."
The Peltola campaign, meanwhile, has called the DOJ's move "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."
"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," said Peltola campaign spokesperson Harry Child.

sources.news_title: 'Twitchy' Blanche skewered for ignoring 'most serious question' of our time in interview
sources.text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche lost his cool on CNN Sunday morning when he was asked whether President Donald Trump is laying the groundwork to contest the midterm elections.
On “State of the Union,” host Dana Bash pressed Blanche on whether Trump is sowing seeds of doubt about the upcoming elections in a way that could lead to something like the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. The question came after DOJ sued Alaska over a second Dan Sullivan appearing on the state’s Senate ballot.
“Oh stop it! You’ve gotta stop it with that!” Blanche said, in a clip shared by journalist Scott MacFarlane.
According to a transcription posted by conservative commentator Eric Daugherty, Blanche went on: “You are not being a real person! That is crazy. Stop, stop, stop.”
Blanche argued that Bash had “set me up” by linking DOJ’s concerns about the Alaska race to Trump doing “something crazy.”
“We’re not laying any groundwork for POTUS to do that, so your premise, your question is not true,” Blanche said, according to Daugherty. He said the department’s “groundwork” in Alaska was meant to determine “if it becomes an issue after the election… whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be.”
Daugherty, the assistant news director at the conservative outlet Florida’s Voice, cheered Blanche’s response. He said the attorney general “just ERUPTED” and added, “I swear, they go to JANUARY 6TH every time.”
Former U.S. Attorney Joyce Vance saw it very differently.
“It’s only the most serious question our democracy faces, so of course the Attorney General of the United States just blows it off,” wrote Vance, a University of Alabama law professor and MS NOW legal analyst who served as U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama under President Barack Obama. “Why bother to go on TV at all this weekend?”
Writer and teacher Andrew Hazlett said, “Blanche is becoming as twitchy and hysteric as Rudy Giuliani.”
Blanche has spent the weekend defending DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit. Critics, including former prosecutors and conservative legal commentators, say the suit’s own filing seeks to block certification of the results, despite Blanche’s insistence that it doesn’t. President Donald Trump has said he ordered the suit filed.

The heated exchange unfolded during a “State of the Union” interview as Bash pressed Blanche over the Justice Department’s decision to sue Alaska ahead of the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections. “[L]et’s just talk turkey,” Bash said, before raising the possibility of a scenario in which President Donald Trump attempts to overturn an election result he disputes, “because one of the big questions is whether or not the president is laying the groundwork for a scenario where — whether it’s Alaska or somewhere else — there is, in your words a couple of days ago, a ‘doomsday scenario,’ and we could be in a situation where President Trump tries to overturn the election, and the result of that could be, God forbid, what we saw after Jan. 6. “I mean— Oh, stop it!” Blanche cut in. “Oh, you got to stop it with that. You are not being a real person. Come on, man.”
Dana Bash asked Attorney General Todd Blanche if DOJ's Alaska lawsuit is groundwork for President Trump to "overturn the election," with a January 6th callback for good measure.

“No,” Bash responded during their crosstalk. “Why are you yelling at me?”

“What I said — and so you have to listen to what I say, or it’s not a fair conversation — what I said is, the groundwork that we are laying is for Alaska,” he added. “[T]he state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be. Trump acknowledged Friday he had directed the Justice Department to pursue the litigation, according to ABC News.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Trump administration's lawsuit to block certification of Alaska's Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race and argued that the legal challenge was a necessary step to avoid confusing voters in the closely watched midterm race.
President Donald Trump, who said Friday that he was "the one that said do it,” is not trying to overturn state election results “in any way, shape or form” on the cusp of the Nov. 3 election, Blanche told CNN's “State of the Union.”
“We wish that we didn’t have to do this. We hope for a resolution that works,” Blanche said.
Republicans fear that a second candidate on the ballot who is named Dan Sullivan — a retired teacher and school administrator from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg — could siphon away votes from the senator and tip the outcome in favor of Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman.
A day after the lawsuit was filed on Thursday, Peltola called it “just flagrant, flagrant corruption in my opinion” and a diversion tactic by Republicans. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, also criticized the lawsuit in a social media post.
Trump told reporters on Sunday that he believed the ballot was illegal because it was unfair and that Sen. Sullivan should be identified to voters as the sitting senator.
“At least let him use the name Sen. Dan Sullivan as opposed to incumbent, because a lot of people don’t know what incumbent means,” Trump said.
Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
Blanche represented Trump as a personal attorney before the Republican president appointed him to lead the Department of Justice, which filed the lawsuit in Alaska. Blanche defended Trump in his election inference case before voters elected Trump to a second White House term, effectively ending the criminal prosecution.
Blanche told CNN host Dana Bash that it was “crazy” for her to ask him if Trump was trying to lay the groundwork for the same sort of election challenges that occurred before a mob of his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
“We are not doing anything improper. We’re not doing anything we’re not allowed to do. And we have to let the process play out," Blanche said. "But I do think it’s important for the American people to understand that we are not — (and) President Trump is not — trying to take over a state election in any way shape or form.”
The lawsuit, he told CBS' “Face the Nation,” is meant to “put guardrails in place” to preserve possible evidence of voter confusion at the polls.
“It’s not saying, ‘Don’t certify.’ It’s saying, ‘If a court ultimately determines that it was decided because of confusion and not the will of the voters, then we do not think the states should certify.’ And that’s consistent with federal law and consistent with even Alaskan law, if that happens,” he said.

The seat is seen as one vital for Republicans if they are to maintain control of the Senate for the second half of President Trump's term in office.
The Justice Department claims that potential confusion over candidates with similar names is the reason for the suit, though some Democrats have argued that it is actually an attempt to interfere in the democratic process.
A ballot with two Sullivans
A candidate on the Nov. 3 ballot is a retired schoolteacher from Petersburg, named Daniel J. Sullivan, with a remarkably similar name to the current Republican senator, Dan Sullivan.
Republicans have accused Daniel J. Sullivan of running as a spoiler to try and divert votes away from the incumbent. The Justice Department has argued in its suit that the name overlap risks confusing voters.
"We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that," Blanche told anchor Dana Bash on CNN's State of the Union, after she asked whether the administration was positioning Trump to overturn a result he did not like.
"President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form," Blanche added.
Tense interview
The exchange grew heated when Bash raised Blanche's "doomsday" remark to reporters in Virginia.
Bash asked Blanche whether the Alaska case risked repeating some of the events during the aftermath of the 2020 election and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol. "Oh, you got to stop it with that. You are not being a real person. Come on, man," Blanche replied, calling the suggestion "crazy."

A state court and the Alaska Supreme Court kept Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot, after Republican election officials in Alaska had sought to remove him on the grounds that his candidacy was to mislead voters intentionally. Trump claims responsibility

Judges skeptical of DOJ effort to force California to set aside suspected noncitizen votes
A three-judge US Circuit Court panel expressed significant skepticism today over the Justice Department’s desire to inject itself into California’s midterm vote-counting process by forcing election officials to set aside the votes of suspected noncitizens who have been issued mail ballots.
During an emergency hearing, 9th Circuit US Court of Appeals Judge Mark Bennett told a Justice Department attorney that California appears to have legal authority to handle its elections on its own, and the fact that Congress passed a criminal law prohibiting noncitizens from voting in federal and state elections doesn’t mean the Justice Department has authority to regulate California’s voting process.
Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, also both questioned the Justice Department’s decision to appeal to the 9th Circuit before the US District Court where the case was originally filed had held a hearing. They pressed DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly about the reliability of the Trump administration’s claims that there are 20,000 noncitizens on California’s voter rolls, information the DOJ has said came from a purchased list of voters and analyzed by third parties.
The Trump administration is attempting to convince the court that it should be able to immediately change California’s ballot processing because of a fear that noncitizens could have sent in votes. The state has already processed more than 300,000 midterm ballots.
But at least two of the three judges on the panel disputed the argument that federal law trumps the Constitution giving the power of running elections primarily to the states.
“It seems to me that under the Elections Clause, they have the right to determine the manner of the elections, including sorting out noncitizens,” Bennett said during the hearing, which was held over videoconference and broadcast on YouTube.

A hearing is now underway in the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals related to the voter roll fight between California and the Trump administration, as the administration continues to double down on claims of voter fraud.
Today’s oral arguments come after the Justice Department sued California and Los Angeles County earlier this month, seeking to prevent officials from counting more than 20,000 mail-in ballots associated with people the government believes are likely noncitizens.

How the hearing will work: Today’s oral arguments are being presented before the following panel: Judge Mark Bennett and Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, both of whom were appointed by President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel Sanchez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden.

Todd Blanche Defends DOJ Alaska Election Lawsuit as Murkowski Pushes Back
sources.text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department’s lawsuit over Alaska’s closely watched Senate election on Saturday, as Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski said the department “should never have filed” the case.
President Donald Trump escalated the dispute in a Truth Social post late Saturday night, attacking Murkowski over her opposition to the lawsuit and calling her “the Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far” and a “DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country.”
Blanche defended the lawsuit again Sunday on CBS News’ Face the Nation, while declining to say whether Trump personally directed him to bring the case.
The legal battle centers on two Senate candidates who share the same first and last names: incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The dispute comes in a race that could help determine control of the Senate.
Blanche said in a post on X that the Justice Department “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.”
“This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead [sic],” Blanche wrote.
The attorney general added: “The lawsuit was written by Justice Department attorneys and the Department did not coordinate with any campaign or candidate, but rather relied solely on federal law.”
The statement comes after Trump said Friday that he had told the DOJ to bring the lawsuit.
Trump has endorsed the incumbent Sullivan and repeatedly alleged that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy was intended to confuse voters and hurt the senator. At a rally in Florida on Friday, Trump called the situation “cheating like hell.”
Newsweek reached out to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign, Senator Sullivan’s campaign, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and the Alaska Division of Elections for comment on Saturday.
Lisa Murkowski Says DOJ ‘Should Never Have Filed’ Alaska Lawsuit
Murkowski, an Alaska Republican who has frequently broken with Trump, pushed back against the lawsuit on Saturday.
“Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” she wrote on X. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”
Trump suggested Murkowski opposed the lawsuit because she wanted Senator Sullivan to lose votes.
“Murkowski probably wants that to happen, which is why she is against the DOJ filing a Lawsuit in order to stop this impending crime and tragedy,” Trump wrote.
On the ballot, the incumbent appears as Dan S. Sullivan and is labeled “Incumbent,” while the other candidate is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
Alaska election officials removed Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the ballot after concluding his candidacy was intended to confuse or mislead voters, but he challenged the decision and was later restored to the ballot by the courts.
Why Is the DOJ Suing Alaska Over the Senate Election?
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit Thursday against Alaska and state election officials, alleging that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy was intended to mislead voters into backing him instead of the incumbent.
The DOJ contends the “sole purpose” of his candidacy is to benefit Peltola by reducing the number of votes cast for Senator Sullivan.
The DOJ is seeking to block certification if Senator Sullivan loses by fewer votes than Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. receives, pending an investigation into potential voter confusion.
On Face the Nation Sunday, Blanche was asked why the Justice Department brought the lawsuit 11 days before the election. He said the DOJ had hoped the Alaska Supreme Court would issue an opinion explaining its reasoning and argued that the court had not considered the federal law on which the department is relying.
Blanche said the DOJ wanted “a procedure in place” in case litigation is brought after the election over potential voter confusion, with ballots preserved so Alaska officials can determine the accurate winner.
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has rejected the suggestion that his candidacy is illegitimate. After he was restored to the ballot earlier this year, he said he was running because he was dissatisfied with the incumbent’s representation.
“It’s a free country,” he said at the time, according to Courthouse News Service. “Most Alaskans are proud Independents and it’s my sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters’ intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running.”
Trump Says He Told DOJ to Bring Alaska Lawsuit
In a Truth Social post Wednesday, Trump called Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy a “SCAM” and said his administration was looking at “powerful legal options” to remove him from the ballot.
After the DOJ filed the case, Trump took credit for the move.
“I’m the one that said ‘do it,’” he told reporters Friday.
Blanche was pressed Sunday on Face the Nation about whom Trump had instructed to bring the lawsuit and whether the president had personally told him to do so.
“I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States,” Blanche said when asked whether Trump had told him directly.
Asked whom Trump was referring to when he said he was “the one that said do it,” Blanche replied: “I have no idea who he was referring to and even if I did have an idea, I would most certainly not talk about it.”
Blanche maintained that the case resulted from DOJ’s own legal work, saying that the department did its “own research under the law” and that its Civil Rights unit drafted the lawsuit before it was filed.
A motion filed seeking dismissal of the lawsuit has since cited Trump’s remark in arguing that the DOJ case was “filed at the behest” of the president. The motion, filed on behalf of two Alaska voters, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause, also asks the court to consider sanctions against the Justice Department attorneys who signed the complaint.
Election-law experts have also questioned the legal basis for the case.
“The DOJ’s lawsuit is completely meritless,” Michael Morley, the Sheila M. McDevitt Professor of Law and faculty director of the Election Law Center at Florida State University, previously told Newsweek.
Mark Brown, a professor at Capital University Law School, also previously told Newsweek that “no federal statute authorizes the relief the DOJ seeks” and called the lawsuit “frivolous.”
Senator Adam Schiff, a California Democrat, also criticized the lawsuit Sunday on NBC News' Meet the Press. When asked whether the DOJ had a point in arguing that the two Sullivans could confuse voters, Schiff said: “No, they don't have a point. And what's more, they don't have standing to bring this kind of a suit. It's not the federal government's business to run Alaskan elections. It's Alaska's business to do that.”
Schiff accused the Justice Department of aiding Trump’s broader effort to challenge election results, saying of Blanche: “This time with Blanche, they're all in on this disgraceful campaign.”
Why the Alaska Senate Race Matters
The dispute comes just days before the November 3 midterm elections, with the Alaska contest among the races that could determine control of the U.S. Senate.
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. Peltola is seeking to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since Mark Begich won in 2008.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and those ballots are redistributed according to voters’ subsequent choices until one candidate has a majority.
Four candidates are competing in the Senate race: Peltola, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Gerald Heikes.

Todd Blanche joins CNN’s State of the Union – October 25, 2026
Attorney General Todd Blanche went off on CNN’s Dana Bash during a fiery interview on Sunday after she attacked the Trump Administration’s lawsuit in Alaska, claiming that Trump is planning another January 6 scenario to overturn the results of the 2026 elections.
The DOJ on Friday sued to block certification of Alaska’s Senate race if the Democrats’ decoy, Daniel J. Sullivan, causes incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan to lose.
Daniel J. Sullivan previously ran in the Senate primary as a Republican and is now running in the general election as a no-party-affiliated candidate after receiving just 2.5% of the vote. He is being propped up to confuse voters into voting for the wrong Dan Sullivan, giving Democrat Mary Peltola a victory in the solid red state.
The lawsuit argues that “some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan.”
“To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the filing says.
The DOJ seeks to prevent certification of the results if “(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”
Blanche argued during an appearance on CNN’s State of the Union that Alaska is “violating federal law and the Constitution by allowing confusion in the ballot” by allowing Daniel J. Sullivan’s dirty trick to proceed.
Bash then ridiculously claimed that “One of the big questions is whether or not the president is laying the groundwork for a scenario where the — whether it’s Alaska or somewhere else there is, in your words, a couple of days ago, a doomsday scenario, and we could be in a situation where President Trump tries to overturn the election, and the result of that could be, God forbid, what we saw after January 6.”
Blanche went off. “Oh, stop it. Oh, you got to stop it with that. You are not being a real person. Come on, man!” he fired back as Bash cried, “Why are you yelling at me?”
“You set me up with the following question. Because the president, because the Department of Justice is concerned that there is an absolute fraud happening in Alaska, and he wants to do something about it — you’re saying, Mr. Attorney General, because the President of the United States wants to stop a fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he going to do something crazy? That is not. That is not a real question.”
Bash continued to accuse Blanche of “laying the groundwork for the president to try to overturn an election that he doesn’t like.”
“We’re not laying any groundwork for the president to do that. So your premise, your question, is not true!” Blanche said. “You have to listen to what I say, or it’s not a fair conversation. What I said is the groundwork that we are laying is for Alaska, for the state of Alaska. If it becomes an issue after the election, we’ll have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be.”
“If the law is broken, and that’s for Alaska and the Alaskan court system to determine if the law is broken, then any state should not certify. I think we can all agree with that,” he added.
Still, Bash continued pushing her January 6, 2027 narrative, despite acknowledging a legal pathway to challenging the results. “I don’t think it’s an unfair question to ask that, given what we saw after the 2020 election,” she said.
“Alaskans are going to go to the ballots potentially confused, which is not something that’s allowed to happen in this country,” Blanche said before nuking Bash again over her obsession with January 6.
“Instead of focusing on how we can address that and how we can remedy that, you’re talking about January 6, okay? And that’s so embarrassing to this network that that’s what you’re talking about.”
“Oh, come on,” Bash interrupted, and Blanche continued, “Don’t ‘Oh, come on,’ me… There’s literally confusion, and then you cite polls. I mean, this isn’t a conversation about polls. It’s not a conversation about January 6. This is a conversation about what’s happening in Alaska right now.”
